# [LumiLettuce] Descriptive & Inferential Statistics

## 0. Load libraries and inspect data set

Load the necessary libraries and create path to tidy data set. Read the tidy data set file in the form of RDS. This is better than .csv version because the RDS can save particular objects. For example, it preserves the variable type of each column making analysis easier.

```{r 00_load}

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(ggplot2)      # to make figures
library(kableExtra)   # to make tables
library(factoextra)   # to make PCA
library(patchwork)
library(car)          # Levene's test
library(vegan)        # For diversity() function
library(ggsignif)
library(rstatix)
library(phyloseq)
library(gt)
library(ggsci)
library(RColorBrewer) # to make figures
library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(circlize)
library(ANCOMBC)
library(mia)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(TreeSummarizedExperiment)
library(ggVennDiagram)
library(indicspecies)
library(forcats)
library(flextable)
library(webshot2)
 

# the RDS file is generated by companion script to tidy data (blueC_data_tidying_R)
lumilettuce <- readRDS("data/processed/full_data.rds") 
    
glimpse(lumilettuce) 
head(lumilettuce)

```

There are 24 columns and 18,988 rows in this data set. It includes both the microbiome data and the metadata. There are categorical and continuous variables.

## I. Abiotic environmental baseline

### Table 1.1 Abiotic summary

Many of the metadata variables are continuous environmental parameters. They help us to understand the context. Some, could also be interesting to explore later on to see if there are correlations in the data associated with these continuous variables. This table compares the metrics (mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range, minimum, and maximum) for the continuous environmental variables of the data set across all diel phases between the two sites. This helps us establish the baseline environmental conditions across sites and time of day.

```{r 01_abiotic_summary}

abiotic_clean <- lumilettuce                                                |>
  filter(
    !is.na(sample_id), 
    !is.na(diel_phase), 
    !is.na(site_name), 
    !is.na(temp_degC), 
    !is.na(salinity_psu), 
    !is.na(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L), 
    !is.na(pH), 
    !is.na(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s)
    )                                                                       |>
  distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE)                                     |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols        = c(temp_degC, 
                    dissolved_oxygen_mg_L, 
                    pH, 
                    salinity_psu,      
                    PAR_umol_photons_m2_s),
           names_to = "Variable",
           values_to = "Value")                                             |>
  # Change the name of the Variable column to make it better suited for a table
  mutate(
    Variable    = case_when(
      Variable  == "temp_degC" ~ "Temperature (°C)",
      Variable  == "dissolved_oxygen_mg_L" ~ "Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)",
      Variable  == "pH" ~ "pH",
      Variable  == "salinity_psu" ~ "Salinity (PSU)",
      Variable  == "PAR_umol_photons_m2_s" ~ "PAR (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹)",
      TRUE ~ Variable)
    )                                                                       |>
  # There will be a top-header and a sub-header for site name and descriptive   
  # statistic variable, respectively
  group_by(diel_phase, Variable, site_name)                                 |>
  summarise(
    Mean        = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), 
    SD          = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Median      = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), 
    IQR         = round(IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Min - Max` = sprintf("%.2f - %.2f", min(Value, na.rm = TRUE), max(Value, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups     = "drop")                                                   |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = site_name,
    values_from = c(Mean, SD, Median, IQR, `Min - Max`),
    names_glue  = "{site_name}_{.value}")                                   |>
 arrange(diel_phase, Variable)                                              |>
  select(
    diel_phase, 
    Variable,
    Pescalgarve_Mean, 
    Pescalgarve_SD, 
    Pescalgarve_Median, 
    Pescalgarve_IQR, 
    `Pescalgarve_Min - Max`,
    `Ria de Alvor_Mean`, 
    `Ria de Alvor_SD`, 
    `Ria de Alvor_Median`, 
    `Ria de Alvor_IQR`, 
    `Ria de Alvor_Min - Max`
  )

abiotic_summary <-  abiotic_clean                                           |>
  select(-diel_phase)                                                       |>
  kbl(
    # Sub-headers for metrics
    col.names   = c("Variable", 
                    "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR", "Min - Max", 
                    "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR", "Min - Max"),
    align       = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_classic(
    full_width  = FALSE, 
    html_font   = "Times New Roman",
    font_size   = 13)                                                       |>
  # Top header spanning across site groups
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Pescalgarve" = 5, "Ria de Alvor" = 5))       |>
  pack_rows("Dawn", 1, 5)                                                   |>
  pack_rows("Noon", 6, 10)                                                  |>
  pack_rows("Dusk", 11, 15)                                                 |>
  pack_rows("Midnight", 16, 20)                                             

# abiotic_summary 

# # Save this table 
# dir.create("../output/tables", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
# 
# save_kable(
#   x    = abiotic_summary,
#   file = "../output/tables/abiotic_summary.png",
#   zoom = 3
# )

```

When comparing between the two sites, we can already see that that the standard variation is 0 at all times for Ria de Alvor, which makes sense because there is a sample size n=1 for all site/diel phase combination. In Ria de Alvor, abiotic parameters were measured a single time per timepoint, whereas Pescalgarve contains independent measurements across tanks (n=3 unique values per diel phase). Dissolved oxygen (DO) and pH are quite similar in both sites. The largest differences for sites are pH, salinity, and PAR.

DO, salinity, and pH remain stable across all time points. PAR varies a lot because it remains low at dawn, dusk, and midnight, with the lowest values at dawn, but then has a peak increase at noon. This pattern is consistent across both sites. Temperature appears to fluctuate slightly during the day.

### Figure 1.1 Multi-faceted abiotic boxplots

The continuous environmental variables temperature, PAR, and salinity showed interesting variation in the table. These boxplots explore the abiotic parameters and how they fluctuate in function of site and time of day.

```{r 02_boxplot_DO}
# Remove NAs
lumilettuce_nowf <- lumilettuce                                            |>
  distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE)                                    |>
  filter(
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    !is.na(sample_type),
    !is.na(morphotype),
    !is.na(site_name), 
    !is.na(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L), 
    !is.na(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s), 
    !is.na(salinity_psu), 
    !is.na(temp_degC), 
    !is.na(temp_degC)
    )                                                                      |>
  # To remove the water samples
  filter(sample_type != "Water filter" | is.na(sample_type)
         ) 

# Boxplot for DO
boxplot_DO <- ggplot(lumilettuce_nowf, aes(x = diel_phase,y = dissolved_oxygen_mg_L, fill = site_name, colour = site_name)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha           = 0.2, # opacity
    outlier.shape   = NA,  # no need to show outliers
    width           = 0.5,
    position        = position_dodge(width=0.75)
  ) +
  # Add a diamond shape for the mean of each box
  stat_summary(
    aes(group       = site_name),           
    fun             = mean,
    geom            = "point",
    shape           = 23,                       
    size            = 3.5,
    colour          = "black",                 
    fill            = "black",                  
    position        = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position        = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width =0.15, dodge.width=0.75),
    size            = 2.5,
    alpha           = 0.3,
  ) +
  # Teal for Pescalgarve and orchid for Ria de Alvor
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Pescalgarve"="#008080", "Ria de Alvor"="#DA70D6")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("Pescalgarve"="#008080", "Ria de Alvor"="#DA70D6")) +
  theme_classic(base_size =12) +
  labs(
    x               = "Diel Phase",
    y               = "Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)",
    fill            = "Site Name",
    colour          = "Site Name"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title      = element_text(face="bold"),
    axis.text       = element_text(colour="black"),
    legend.position = "right",
    lengend.title   = element_text(face="bold")
  )

# Display DO boxplot
boxplot_DO

# Save the DO boxplot
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/boxplot_DO.png",
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)


```

There are 9 observations for each box with 3 unique values for each box of Pescalgarve. A black diamond symbolizing the mean was added to each box. Ria de Alvor only has 9 of the same measurements (repeated) for each diel phase.

Pescalgarve has a slight increase in DO at dusk, whereas the other diel phases appear stable at around 10 mg/L. Ria de Alvor shows a greater increase at noon and dusk before going back down at midnight. Ria de Alvor varies between 9 and 11 mg/L.

This will generate one figure with all the abiotic variable boxplots and only show the legend once to avoid repetitions.

```{r 07_multi_abiotic_boxplot}

# Generate standardized boxplots
create_env_boxplot <- function(data, y_var, y_label) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = diel_phase, y = .data[[y_var]], fill = site_name, colour = site_name)) +
    geom_boxplot(
      alpha         = 0.2,
      outlier.shape = NA,
      width         = 0.5,
      position      = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
    ) +
    stat_summary(
      aes(group     = site_name),
      fun           = mean,
      geom          = "point",
      shape         = 23,
      size          = 3.5,
      colour        = "black",
      fill          = "black",
      position      = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
    ) +
    geom_point(
      position      = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.75),
      size          = 2.5,
      alpha         = 0.3
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6")) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      x             = "Diel Phase",
      y             = y_label,
      fill          = "Site Name",
      colour        = "Site Name"
    ) +
    theme(
      axis.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text     = element_text(colour = "black"),
      legend.title  = element_text(face = "bold", size = 25),
      legend.text   = element_text(size = 20),
      # Add a solid border, light background, and padding around the legend box
      legend.box.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9, fill = "grey"),
      legend.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 12, b = 10, l = 12)
    )
}

# Create the 5 individual subplots
p_do   <- create_env_boxplot(lumilettuce_nowf, "dissolved_oxygen_mg_L", "Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)")
p_par  <- create_env_boxplot(lumilettuce_nowf, "PAR_umol_photons_m2_s", expression(bold(paste("PAR (", mu, "mol photons m"^-2*" s"^-1*")"))))
p_sal  <- create_env_boxplot(lumilettuce_nowf, "salinity_psu", "Salinity (PSU)")
p_temp <- create_env_boxplot(lumilettuce_nowf, "temp_degC", "Temperature (°C)")
p_ph   <- create_env_boxplot(lumilettuce_nowf, "pH", "pH")

# Assemble with patchwork
# guide_area() fills the 6th slot with the collected legend
# tag_levels supplies A-E for the 5 plots and leaves the 6th empty 
multi_abiotic_boxplot <- (p_do + p_par + p_sal + p_temp + p_ph + guide_area()) +
  plot_layout(
    ncol            = 3,
    nrow            = 2,
    guides          = "collect"
  ) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels      = list(c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "")),
    theme           = theme(
      plot.tag      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
    )
  ) &
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside"
  )

print(multi_abiotic_boxplot)

# Save
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/multipanel_environmental_boxplots.png",
  plot     = multi_abiotic_boxplot,
  width    = 13,
  height   = 8.5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

### Test 1.1 Mann-Whitney U test & Kruskal-Wallis

First, I will verify whether my data is normally distributed for each environmental variable using the Shapiro-Wilk test. The null hypothesis (if the p-value is greater than 0.05) states that the data is normally distributed. Then, I will test for the homogeneity of variances. The null hypothesis states that the variances are equal across all groups. If the data is parametric, i will perform a Two-Way ANOVA. If not, I will perform a Mann-Whitney U Test for site_name (2 levels) and a Kruskal-Wallis for diel_phase (4 levels). I can then perform a Dunn test to see where the significant differences are.

```{r 08_abiotic_test}
# Check for normality using Shapiro-Wilk test
shapiro.test(lumilettuce_nowf$dissolved_oxygen_mg_L) # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(lumilettuce_nowf$PAR_umol_photons_m2_s) # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(lumilettuce_nowf$salinity_psu)          # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(lumilettuce_nowf$temp_degC)             # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(lumilettuce_nowf$pH)                    # data is not normally distributed

# Create boxplots for both variables to see whether there are outliers
boxplot(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf) # outliers
boxplot(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf)  # no outliers

boxplot(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf) # outliers
boxplot(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf)  # outliers

boxplot(salinity_psu ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf) # outliers
boxplot(salinity_psu ~ site_name, data =lumilettuce_nowf)  #  no outliers

boxplot(temp_degC ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf) # outliers
boxplot(temp_degC ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf)  #  no outliers

boxplot(pH ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf) # outliers
boxplot(pH ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf)  #  no outliers

# Perform Levene's test for homogeneity of variances
# Use center = median if there are outliers (more robust)

leveneTest(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = median) # not equal
leveneTest(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = mean)  # not equal

leveneTest(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = median) # not equal
leveneTest(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = median) # equal

leveneTest(salinity_psu ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = median) # equal
leveneTest(salinity_psu ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = mean) # not equal

leveneTest(temp_degC ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = median) # not equal
leveneTest(temp_degC ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = mean) # not equal

leveneTest(pH ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = median) # equal
leveneTest(pH ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, center = mean) # not equal

# Mann-Whitney U test for site_nmae
wilcox.test(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, exact = FALSE) # significant diff
wilcox.test(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, exact = FALSE) # no diff
wilcox.test(salinity_psu ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, exact = FALSE)          # significant diff
wilcox.test(temp_degC ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, exact = FALSE)             # significant diff
wilcox.test(pH ~ site_name, data = lumilettuce_nowf, exact = FALSE)                    # significant diff

# Kruskal-Wallis test for diel_phase
kruskal.test(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf)              # significant diff
kruskal.test(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf)              # significant diff
kruskal.test(salinity_psu ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf)                       # no diff
kruskal.test(temp_degC ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf)                          # no diff   
kruskal.test(pH ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf)                                 # significant diff

# Dunn test for significantly different variables
dunn_test(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, p.adjust.method = "holm") # dawn and dusk
dunn_test(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, p.adjust.method = "holm")
dunn_test(pH ~ diel_phase, data = lumilettuce_nowf, p.adjust.method = "holm")

```

All the p-values for the Shapiro-Wilk test are smaller than 0.05, which means that I must reject the null hypothesis. This means that the data is not normally distributed. The homogeneity of variances also fails in most cases. Because the abiotic parameters showed non-normal data and heterogeneous variances across groups, non-parametric Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests were conducted. Mann-Whitney U test showed significant difference between both sites for all variables except PAR.

The Kruskal-Wallis test showed significant difference between diel phases for DO, PAR, and pH.

The Dunn test shows that the significant difference for DO is between dawn and dusk, which is consistent with the previous box plot. For PAR, the largest significant differences are between dawn and noon and noon and midnight, then between dusk and midnight, and finally between noon and dusk. For pH, the largest significant difference is between noon and midnight, then dawn and noon, and finally noon and dusk.

### Figure 1.2 Principal component analysis abiotic variables

This principal component analysis (PCA) looks at the five (5) abiotic variables and the two sites. The direction and length of the arrows indicates how strongly each variable correlates with the axes and with each other.

