
The first two principle components account for 67.3% of the total variance, which is adequate. The primary drivers of Dim1 (39.2%) are dissolved oxygen and pH. The primary drivers of Dim2 (28.1%) are temperature and salinity, with PAR also playing a smaller role. The samples from Pescalgarve clustered almost exclusively in the negative values of Dim2 which means that suggests that they are characterized by lower temperature and salinity. Ria de Alvor samples are fewer and clustered in the positive values of Dim2, characterized by higher temperatures and salinities. Pescalgarve samples also span across a wide range of Dim1 and Dim2 suggesting greater environmental variability than the tighter cluster of Ria de Alvor. This suggests Ria de Alvor has a more stable and homogeneous environment than Pescalgarve.

## II. Host selection: *Ulva* epibiome vs. surrounding bacterioplankton

### Figure 2.1 Taxonomic stacked barplot *Ulva* and seawater

This is a broad taxonomic stacked barplot for the relative abundance between *Ulva* and seawater across sites. The bacteria are shown at the order level. This allows us to have a quick overview of which bacterial orders are found in both water filter samples and the seaweed, and which are unique to the seaweed host.

```{r 10_barplot_ulva_seawater}

# Filter data for valid sites, and sample types 
bacteria_data <- lumilettuce                                                     |>
  filter(!is.na(order), order != "", order != "unknown", order != "Unclassified")|>
  filter(sample_type %in% c("Ulva", "Water filter"), !is.na(site_name), !is.na(genus), superkingdom == "Bacteria") 

# Top 10 most abundant bacterial orders across bacteria_data
top_10_orders <- bacteria_data                                                   |>
  group_by(order)                                                                |>
  summarise(total_count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")            |>
  slice_max(order_by = total_count, n = 10)                                      |>
  pull(order)

# Group lower-abundance orders into "Other" and calculate relative abundance (%)
order_rel_abund <- bacteria_data                                                 |>
  mutate(
    order_grouped = if_else(order %in% top_10_orders, order, "Other (< 2%)")
  )                                                                              |>
  group_by(site_name, sample_type, order_grouped)                                |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last")             |>
  mutate(relative_abundance = (count / sum(count)) * 100)                        |>
  ungroup()                                                                      |>
  # Reorder factors so "Other" is at the bottom of the stack and dominant orders are on top
  mutate(
    order_grouped = factor(
      order_grouped,
      levels = c("Other (< 2%)", rev(top_10_orders))
    )
  )

# Custom distinct color palette 
custom_colors <- c(
  "Other (< 2%)"       = "#D3D3D3",
  "Pseudomonadales"    = "#1F77B4",
  "Flavobacteriales"   = "#FF7F0E",
  "Enterobacterales"   = "#2CA02C",
  "Cytophagales"       = "#D62728",
  "Chitinophagales"    = "#9467BD",
  "Bacteroidales"      = "#8C564B",
  "Rhodobacterales"    = "#E377C2",
  "Caulobacterales"    = "#7F7F7F",
  "Sphingobacteriales" = "#BCBD22",
  "Burkholderiales"    = "#17BECF"
)

# Create the stacked barplot
barplot_ulva_seawater <- ggplot(
  order_rel_abund, 
  aes(
    x = sample_type, 
    y = relative_abundance, 
    fill = order_grouped)
  ) +
  geom_bar(
    stat = "identity", 
    position = "stack", 
    width = 0.65, 
    colour = "black", 
    linewidth = 0.25
    ) +
  facet_wrap(~site_name) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors, guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02)), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    x    = "Sample Type",
    y    = "Relative Abundance (%)",
    fill = "Microbial Order"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.title        = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text         = element_text(colour = "black", size = 11),
    strip.text        = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    strip.background  = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = "grey93", linewidth = 0.6),
    legend.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text       = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position   = "right",
    panel.spacing     = unit(1.5, "lines")
  )


print(barplot_ulva_seawater)


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/barplot_ulva_seawater.png",
  plot     = barplot_ulva_seawater,
  width    = 9.5,
  height   = 6,
  dpi      = 300
)


```

We can see from this barplot that the two dominant bacterial orders are Pseudomonadales and Flavobacteriales for both sample types at both sites. At Pescalgarve, the *Ulva* samples contain more Cytophagales than in the water filter sample. This suggests that *Ulva* recruits this order specifically. The same is seen in the samples collected at Ria de Alvor. In the seaweed sample of Ria de Alvor, we see less Flavobacteriales than in the water filter sample. The Pescalgarve seaweed sample also has more Chitinophagales than in the respective water filter sample.

### Figure 2.2 Alpha diversity comparison

The alpha diversity analysis helps portray the bacterial community in both sites and in both sample types. Three comparisons are performed here: observed species richness, Shannon's diversity index (H'), and Pielou's evenness (J').

```{r 11_combined_site_alpha}

# Calculate alpha diversity metrics per sample_id
alpha_metrics <- bacteria_data |>
  group_by(sample_id, sample_type, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  summarise(
    Observed_Richness          = n_distinct(genus),
    Shannon                    = diversity(count, index = "shannon"),
    Evenness                   = Shannon / log(Observed_Richness),
    .groups                    = "drop"
  )

print(alpha_metrics)


# Create boxplot function
create_alpha_boxplot <- function(data, y_var, y_label) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = sample_type, y = .data[[y_var]], fill = sample_type, colour = sample_type)) +
    geom_boxplot(
      alpha                    = 0.3,
      outlier.shape            = NA,
      width                    = 0.45,
      colour                   = "black",
      linewidth                = 0.6
    ) +
    # Add diamond shape for the mean
    stat_summary(
      fun                      = mean,
      geom                     = "point",
      shape                    = 23,
      size                     = 3.5,
      colour                   = "black",
      fill                     = "black"
    ) +
    geom_jitter(
      width                    = 0.15,
      size                     = 2.5,
      alpha                    = 0.6
    ) +
    # Color scheme: green for Ulva, blue for seawater
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#2E8B57", "Water filter" = "#4682B4")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#2E8B57", "Water filter" = "#4682B4")) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      x                       = "Sample Type",
      y                       = y_label,
      fill                    = "Sample Type",
      colour                  = "Sample Type"
    ) +
    theme(
      axis.title              = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text               = element_text(colour = "black", size = 11),
      legend.position         = "none" 
    )
}


# Generate the 3 individual alpha diversity subplots
p_richness <- create_alpha_boxplot(alpha_metrics, "Observed_Richness", "Observed Genus Richness")
p_shannon  <- create_alpha_boxplot(alpha_metrics, "Shannon", "Shannon Diversity Index (H')")
p_evenness <- create_alpha_boxplot(alpha_metrics, "Evenness", "Pielou's Evenness (J')")


# Create a faceted boxplot function comparing Ulva vs seawater across both sites
create_faceted_alpha <- function(data, y_var, y_label) {
  create_alpha_boxplot(data, y_var, y_label) +
    facet_wrap(~site_name) +
    theme(
      strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      strip.background = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = "grey93", linewidth = 0.5)
    )
}

# Create the faceted plots
p_rich_site <- create_faceted_alpha(alpha_metrics, "Observed_Richness", "Observed Genus Richness")
p_shan_site <- create_faceted_alpha(alpha_metrics, "Shannon", "Shannon Diversity Index (H')")
p_even_site <- create_faceted_alpha(alpha_metrics, "Evenness", "Pielou's Evenness (J')")

# Patchwork all the plots
combined_site_alpha <- (p_rich_site / p_shan_site / p_even_site) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

print(combined_site_alpha)


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/alpha_diversity_ulva_vs_seawater.png",
  plot     = combined_site_alpha,
  width    = 8,
  height   = 10,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

The observed genus richness appears to be similar between sample types from Pescalgarve, but not in Ria de Alvor. The Shannon diversity index appears to be the same for both sample types in Pescalgarve again, but a slight difference for the water filter samples at Ria de Alvor. The evenness seems very similar across sample type and site.

### Test 2.1 Mann-Whitney U Test

First, I will verify whether my data is normally distributed for each environmental variable using the Shapiro-Wilk test. The null hypothesis (if the p-value is greater than 0.05) states that the data is normally distributed. Then, I will test for the homogeneity of variances. The null hypothesis states that the variances are equal across all groups. If the data is parametric, i will perform a Two-Way ANOVA. If not, I will perform a Mann-Whitney U Test for site_name (2 levels) and sample type (2 levels).

```{r 12_mann_whitney_alpha}

shapiro.test(alpha_metrics$Observed_Richness) # not normally distributed
shapiro.test(alpha_metrics$Shannon)           # not normally distributed
shapiro.test(alpha_metrics$Evenness)          # not normally distributed

boxplot(Observed_Richness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
boxplot(Observed_Richness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers

boxplot(Shannon ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
boxplot(Shannon ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
               
boxplot(Evenness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
boxplot(Evenness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
# They all have outliers, so it is better to use the median as the center (more robust) for Levene's test

leveneTest(Observed_Richness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous
leveneTest(Observed_Richness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous

leveneTest(Shannon ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous
leveneTest(Shannon ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # homogeneous

leveneTest(Evenness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous
leveneTest(Evenness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # homogeneous
# The data is not parametric, Mann-Whitney U test must be performed

wilcox.test(Observed_Richness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Observed_Richness ~ sample_type, data = filter(alpha_metrics, site_name == "Pescalgarve"), exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Observed_Richness ~ sample_type, data = filter(alpha_metrics, site_name == "Ria de Alvor"), exact = FALSE) # significant difference

wilcox.test(Shannon ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Shannon ~ sample_type, data = filter(alpha_metrics, site_name == "Pescalgarve"), exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Shannon ~ sample_type, data = filter(alpha_metrics, site_name == "Ria de Alvor"), exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Evenness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Evenness ~ sample_type, data = filter(alpha_metrics, site_name == "Pescalgarve"), exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Evenness ~ sample_type, data = filter(alpha_metrics, site_name == "Ria de Alvor"), exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

               
```

When pooling samples across both localities, global Mann-Whitney U tests indicated no significant difference in observed genus richness, Shannon diversity, or Pielou's evenness between *Ulva* and the surrounding seawater (p \> 0.05). However, site-specific analyses revealed that this aggregate parity masked contrasting local dynamics. In the Ria de Alvor, the seaweed supports a significantly richer bacterial community than the surrounding seawater (p = 0.0256). In contrast, at Pescalgarve, background seawater richness was not significantly different from the seaweed's (p = 0.1004). Shannon's diversity and Pielou's evenness remained consistent across sample types at both sites.

### Figure 2.3 Principal coordinates analysis

This section investigates the beta diversity ordination of bacterial communities between *Ulva* and seawater across sites. These plots are based on abundance-weighed Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and incidence-based Jaccard distance.

```{r 13_pcoa_ulva_water}

# Extract sample-level metadata
metadata_pcoa <- bacteria_data                                                |>
  distinct(sample_id, sample_type, site_name, diel_phase)                     |>
  arrange(sample_id)

comm_matrix <- bacteria_data                                                  |>
  # Sum duplicate genus counts per sample first
  group_by(sample_id, genus)                                                  |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")               |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from                   = genus,
    values_from                  = count,
    values_fill                  = 0
  )                                                                           |>
  arrange(sample_id)                                                          |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# Make sure the metadata matches community matrix rows exactly
metadata_pcoa <- metadata_pcoa                                                          |> 
  filter(sample_id %in% rownames(comm_matrix))

# Bray-Curtis (abundance-weighted)
dist_bc <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "bray")
pcoa_bc <- cmdscale(dist_bc, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

var_bc_1 <- round((pcoa_bc$eig[1] / sum(pcoa_bc$eig[pcoa_bc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)
var_bc_2 <- round((pcoa_bc$eig[2] / sum(pcoa_bc$eig[pcoa_bc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)

df_pcoa_bc <- data.frame(
  sample_id = rownames(pcoa_bc$points),
  PCoA1     = pcoa_bc$points[, 1],
  PCoA2     = pcoa_bc$points[, 2]
)                                                                             |>
  dplyr::left_join(metadata_pcoa, by = "sample_id")

# Jaccard (presence-absence / incidence-based)
dist_jacc <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
pcoa_jacc <- cmdscale(dist_jacc, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

var_jacc_1 <- round((pcoa_jacc$eig[1] / sum(pcoa_jacc$eig[pcoa_jacc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)
var_jacc_2 <- round((pcoa_jacc$eig[2] / sum(pcoa_jacc$eig[pcoa_jacc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)

df_pcoa_jacc <- data.frame(
  sample_id = rownames(pcoa_jacc$points),
  as.data.frame(pcoa_jacc$points),                               
  PCoA1     = pcoa_jacc$points[, 1],
  PCoA2     = pcoa_jacc$points[, 2]
)                                                                             |>
  dplyr::left_join(metadata_pcoa, by = "sample_id")

# Create a function to plot PCoA ordinations
plot_pcoa <- function(df, var1, var2, dist_name) {
  ggplot(
    df,   
    aes(
      x                          = PCoA1, 
      y                          = PCoA2, 
      colour                     = sample_type, 
      fill                       = sample_type, 
      shape                      = site_name
      )
    ) +
    # 95% normal confidence ellipses around sample types
    stat_ellipse(
      aes(group                  = sample_type),
      geom                       = "polygon",
      alpha                      = 0.15,
      type                       = "t",
      level                      = 0.95,
      show.legend                = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_point(size = 3.5, alpha = 0.85, stroke = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#006400", "Water filter" = "#008ECC")) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#006400", "Water filter" = "#008ECC")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = 16, "Ria de Alvor" = 17)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      title                      = paste("PCoA -", dist_name),
      x                          = paste0("PCoA1 (", var1, "%)"),
      y                          = paste0("PCoA2 (", var2, "%)"),
      colour                     = "Sample Type",
      fill                       = "Sample Type",
      shape                      = "Site Name"
    ) +
    theme(
      plot.title                 = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5),
      axis.title                 = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text                  = element_text(colour = "black"),
      legend.title               = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position            = "right",
      legend.box.background      = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5, fill = "grey98"),
      legend.margin              = margin(6, 8, 6, 8)
    )
}

# Generate individual PCoA plots
p_bc   <- plot_pcoa(df_pcoa_bc, var_bc_1, var_bc_2, "Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity")
p_jacc <- plot_pcoa(df_pcoa_jacc, var_jacc_1, var_jacc_2, "Jaccard Distance (Presence-Absence)")

# Combine multi-panel figure 
pcoa_ulva_water <- (p_bc + p_jacc) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2, guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels                   = "A",
    theme                        = theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

print(pcoa_ulva_water)

dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/pcoa_ulva_water.png",
  plot     = pcoa_ulva_water,
  width    = 12,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

There is a lot of overlap in both plots. This suggests that the surrounding planktonic bacteria share core taxonomic members with the algal surface. The principal coordinates explain a low percentage of total community variance.

### Test 2.2 PERMANOVA

This PERMANOVA tests whether community composition varied by sampling site and sample type between the water filter and seaweed samples.

```{r 14_permanova_ulva_water}

# Create the community matrix with id_cols = sample_id
comm_matrix <- bacteria_data                                                  |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus)                                                  |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")               |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols                 = sample_id,
    names_from              = genus,
    values_from             = count,
    values_fill             = 0
  )                                                                           |>
  arrange(sample_id)                                                          |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")                                             |>
  as.matrix() 

# Check that it is numeric
is.numeric(comm_matrix) # returns TRUE

# Abundance-weighted Bray-Curtis
dist_bray <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "bray")

# Incidence-based Jaccard
dist_jacc <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE)


cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: BRAY-CURTIS ===================\n")
permanova_bray <- adonis2(
  dist_bray ~ sample_type * site_name,
  data         = metadata_pcoa,
  permutations = 999,
  by           = "margin"
)
print(permanova_bray)

cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: JACCARD ===================\n")
permanova_jacc <- adonis2(
  dist_jacc ~ sample_type * site_name,
  data         = metadata_pcoa,
  permutations = 999,
  by           = "margin"
)
print(permanova_jacc)


# Test homogeneity of multivariate dispersion (betadisper)
# Tests if within-group variance differs (helps validate PERMANOVA results)

cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Sample Type (Bray-Curtis) ---\n")
disp_type <- betadisper(dist_bray, metadata_pcoa$sample_type)
print(anova(disp_type))

cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Site Name (Bray-Curtis) ---\n")
disp_site <- betadisper(dist_bray, metadata_pcoa$site_name)
print(anova(disp_site))

# Visualize dispersions
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(disp_type, main = "Dispersion: Sample Type")
plot(disp_site, main = "Dispersion: Site Name")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

This means that the community composition varied significantly by sampling site and sample type.

## III. The core microbiome of *Ulva*

### Figure 3.1 The core microbiome venn diagram

This Venn diagram shows the partitioning of persistent bacterial taxa (with a prevalence equal or greater than 70%) associated with *Ulva* between the natural lagoon and the land-based aquaculture facility.

```{r 15_venn_diagram}
# Prepare the full dataset (Ulva + water filter)
ind_data <- lumilettuce                                                         |>
  filter(
    superkingdom          == "Bacteria",
    sample_type %in% c("Ulva", "Water filter"),
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    !is.na(genus),
    !is.na(sample_type),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    count > 0
  )

# Build community matrix 
comm_all <- ind_data                                                            |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus)                                                    |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")                 |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = genus, values_from = count, values_fill = 0)         |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# Metadata matched to matrix rows
meta_all <- ind_data                                                            |>
  distinct(sample_id, sample_type, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  arrange(match(sample_id, rownames(comm_all)))

# Community matrix for Ulva only (for site and diel testing on the host)
ulva_ids <- meta_all                                                            |> 
  filter(sample_type == "Ulva")                                                 |> 
  pull(sample_id)
comm_ulva <- comm_all[ulva_ids, ]
meta_ulva <- meta_all                                                           |> 
  filter(sample_id %in% ulva_ids)

# Convert counts to relative abundance (%)
rel_abund_ulva <- comm_ulva / rowSums(comm_ulva) * 100

# Extract core taxa per site or globally
get_core_taxa <- function(mat, prev_thresh = 0.70, abund_thresh = 0.01) {
  # Fraction of samples where relative abundance exceeds threshold
  prev <- colMeans(mat > abund_thresh)
  names(prev[prev >= prev_thresh])
}

# Define core at 70% prevalence and > 0.01% relative abundance
core_global <- get_core_taxa(rel_abund_ulva, prev_thresh = 0.70)

# Site-specific core
pesc_samples <- meta_ulva                                                       |> 
  filter(site_name== "Pescalgarve")                                             |> 
  pull(sample_id)
alvor_samples <- meta_ulva                                                      |> 
  filter(site_name == "Ria de Alvor")                                           |> 
  pull(sample_id)

core_pesc  <- get_core_taxa(rel_abund_ulva[pesc_samples, ], prev_thresh = 0.70)
core_alvor <- get_core_taxa(rel_abund_ulva[alvor_samples, ], prev_thresh = 0.70)

# Taxa shared across both environments
core_shared <- intersect(core_pesc, core_alvor)

# Output summary
list(
  Total_Core_Pescalgarve = length(core_pesc),
  Total_Core_Alvor       = length(core_alvor),
  Shared_Ubiquitous_Core = core_shared
)

# Combine core taxa into a named list
core_list <- list(
  "Pescalgarve"          = core_pesc,
  "Ria de Alvor"         = core_alvor
)

# Build the Venn Diagram
venn_plot <- ggVennDiagram(
  core_list,
  label                  = "both",
  label_percent_digit    = 1,
  label_size             = 4.5,
  label_color            = "black",
  label_alpha            = 0,
  edge_size              = 1.2,
  set_size               = 5
) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low                  = "#F7FBFF",
    high                 = "#6BAED6",
    name                 = "Number of\nTaxa"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values               = c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6")
  ) +
  # Expand coordinate limits to prevent text truncation on the left and right
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.25, 0.25))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.15, 0.15))) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title           = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, size = 14, margin = margin(b = 4)),
    plot.subtitle        = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 11, colour = "grey30", margin = margin(b = 10)),
    legend.position      = "right",
    legend.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    plot.margin          = margin(t = 20, r = 30, b = 20, l = 30, unit = "pt")
  )

print(venn_plot)

dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/venn_diagram.png",
  plot     = venn_plot,
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)


```

The majority of core bacterial taxa (57.7%) are found in both sites. This means that most of the epibiome is recruited by the *Ulva* host regardless of whether it grows in the open coastal lagoon. In addition, approximately one quarter of the persistent taxa is exclusive to the natural lagoon. In total, Ria de Alvor supports 114 core taxa (35 + 79 taxa). Pescalgarve contains fewer persistent taxa (16.8%), making up 102 taxa in total. Across both habitats, 137 unique bacterial taxa meet the core threshold.

## IV. Locality & thallus morphology

### Test 4.1 PERMANOVA morphology

```{r 16_permanova_morph}
morph_data <- lumilettuce                                                       |>
  filter(
    superkingdom           == "Bacteria",
    sample_type            == "Ulva",
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(genus),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    !is.na(morphotype),
    count > 0
  )

# Metadata aligned to samples
meta_morph <- morph_data                                                        |>
  distinct(sample_id, site_name, morphotype)                                    |>
  arrange(sample_id)

# Community abundance matrix 
comm_morph <- morph_data                                                        |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus)                                                    |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")                 |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols                = sample_id,
    names_from             = genus,
    values_from            = count,
    values_fill            = 0
  )                                                                             |>
  arrange(sample_id)                                                            |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")                                               |>
  as.matrix()

# Confirm identical sample order
stopifnot(identical(rownames(comm_morph), meta_morph$sample_id))

# Compute dissimilarity and run PERMANOVA
dist_bc_morph <- vegdist(comm_morph, method = "bray")

permanova_morph <- adonis2(
  dist_bc_morph ~ site_name + morphotype,
  data                     = meta_morph,
  permutations             = 999,
  by                       = "margin"
)

print(permanova_morph)

```

The analysis is based on 72 samples in total. Site effect significantly shapes the *Ulva* epibiome (F = 10.88), R2 = 0.116, p = 0.001) and accounts for 11.6% of the total community variation after partialling out morphotype. Morphotype also significantly shapes the epibiome (F = 7.36, R2 = 0.157, p = 0.001), explaining 15.7% of the variation. The residual variation is very high at 72.7%, but this is expected for high-resolution microbial field ecology where micro-environmental fluctuations, sequencing depth variation, and individual-level host heterogeneity exist.

### Figure 4.1 Principal coordinate analysis morphology

This is a PCoA of *Ulva* bacterial communities across distinct thallus morphotypes and diel phases. The ordination is based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities computed from bacterial genus abundances across 72 *Ulva* thallus samples. The axes represent the percentage of multivariate variance explained by PCoA1 and PCoA2. The dasked polygons indicate 95% confidence ellipses for each morphological group.

```{r 17_pcoa_morphotype}
# Calculate PCoA 
pcoa_res <- cmdscale(dist_bc_morph, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Calculate percentage of variance explained by each axis
var_exp <- round((pcoa_res$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa_res$eig[pcoa_res$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)

# Pull metadata directly from morph_data where diel_phase exists
pcoa_df <- data.frame(
  sample_id                  = rownames(pcoa_res$points),
  PCoA1                      = pcoa_res$points[, 1],
  PCoA2                      = pcoa_res$points[, 2]
)                                                                               |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    morph_data                                                                  |> 
      dplyr::distinct(sample_id, site_name, morphotype, diel_phase),
    by = "sample_id"
  )

# Build PCoA Plot
pcoa_morphotype <- ggplot(pcoa_df, aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2)) +
  stat_ellipse(
    aes(color = morphotype, fill = morphotype),
    geom                     = "polygon",
    alpha                    = 0.12,
    level                    = 0.95,
    linetype                 = "dashed",
    show.legend              = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(fill = morphotype, color = morphotype, shape = diel_phase),
    size                     = 4.5,
    stroke                   = 0.9,
    alpha                    = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values                   = c(
      "Blade"                = "#800020",
      "Narrow thalli"        = "#BDB76B",
      "Filamentous"          = "#C8A2C8"
    )
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Blade"                = "#800020",
      "Narrow thalli"        = "#BDB76B",
      "Filamentous"          = "#C8A2C8"
    )
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      "Dawn"                 = 24, # Triangle Up (fillable)
      "Noon"                 = 21, # Circle (fillable)
      "Dusk"                 = 25, # Triangle Down (fillable)
      "Midnight"             = 8   # Star
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x                        = paste0("PCoA 1 (", var_exp[1], "%)"),
    y                        = paste0("PCoA 2 (", var_exp[2], "%)"),
    color                    = "Morphotype",
    fill                     = "Morphotype",
    shape                    = "Time of Day"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.title               = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text                = element_text(color = "black"),
    panel.grid.minor         = element_blank(),
    panel.border             = element_rect(color = "grey80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.6),
    legend.position          = "right",
    legend.box               = "vertical",
    legend.title             = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text              = element_text(size = 9)
  ) +
  guides(
    fill  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21, size = 4)),
    color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21, size = 4)),
    shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3.8, stroke = 1))
  )

print(pcoa_morphotype)

dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/pcoa_morphotype.png",
  plot     = pcoa_morphotype,
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 6,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

The first thing that is striking about this figure is the pronounced divergence of the filamentous morphotype along PCoA2 (expalining 19.1% of total variation). It has less ellipse overlap than the other two morphotypes that cluster together toward negative PCoA2 coordinates. This could be because filamentous *Ulva* thalli have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratios compared to broad blade or tubular ribbons. Although the blade and narrow thalli morphotypes overlap extensively, the blade morphotype has a wider distribution along PCoA1 (21.6% of variation), which suggests greater community heterogeneity and stronger susceptibility to environmental fluctuations across sites. Also, the four diel sampling periods (Dawn, Noon, Dusk, and Midnight) seem spread randomly rather than clustering into temporal sub-clusters.

## V. Temporal stability across diel cycle

### Figure 5.1 Order stacked barplots by site and diel phase

This barplot is looking at the relative abundance (%) of orders for each diel phase in both environments. It shows only the 10 dominant orders and the rest is categorized as "Other".

```{r 18_barplot_order_diel}

# Remove water filter and mock community sample
ulva_clean <- lumilettuce                                                      |>
  filter(
    !is.na(site_name), 
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    sample_type == "Ulva" | (sample_type != "Water filter" & !str_ends(sample_id, regex("w", ignore_case = TRUE))),
    sample_id != "CM"
  )                                                                            |>
  mutate(order = replace_na(as.character(order), "Unassigned"))

# Identify the top 10 bacterial orders across all samples
top_10_orders <- ulva_clean                                                    |>
  group_by(order)                                                              |>
  summarise(total = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")                |>
  filter(order != "Unassigned")                                                |>
  slice_max(order_by = total, n = 10)                                          |>
  pull(order)

order_data_diel <- ulva_clean |>
  mutate(order_top = if_else(order %in% top_10_orders, order, "Other"))        |>
  # Sum counts per sample and order
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, order_top)                        |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last")           |>
  # Compute relative abundance (%) per sample
  mutate(rel_abund = (count / sum(count)) * 100)                               |>
  ungroup()                                                                    |>
  # Fill in zeros for unobserved orders per sample while preserving site and phase
  complete(
    nesting(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase),
    order_top,
    fill = list(count = 0, rel_abund = 0)
  )                                                                            |>
  # Compute the mean relative abundance across replicates for each site and diel phase
  group_by(site_name, diel_phase, order_top)                                   |>
  summarise(mean_rel_abund = mean(rel_abund, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last")                                                                                |>
  # Re-normalize to ensure 100% stack per diel phase
  mutate(mean_rel_abund = (mean_rel_abund / sum(mean_rel_abund)) * 100)        |>
  ungroup()                                                                    |>
  mutate(
    diel_phase = factor(diel_phase),
    order_top  = factor(order_top, levels = c(top_10_orders, "Other")),
    order_top  = forcats::fct_relevel(order_top, "Other", after = Inf)
  )

head(order_data_diel)

# Create the plot 
ggplot(order_data_diel, aes(x = diel_phase, y = mean_rel_abund, fill = order_top))         +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2, width = 0.8)              +
  facet_wrap(~ site_name)                                                                  +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100.1), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25))     +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette       = "Paired")                                              + 
  theme_minimal(base_size         = 12)                                                    +
  labs(
    y                             = "Mean Relative Abundance (%)", 
    x                             = "Diel Phase", 
    fill                          = "Order"
  )                                                                                        +
  theme(
    axis.title                    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text                     = element_text(color = "black"),
    strip.text                    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position               = "right",
    legend.title                  = element_text(face = "bold")
  )


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/barplot_order_diel.png",
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)

```

From this, we can see that Pseudomonadale*s* is the dominant order in Ria de Alvor at all diel phases. In Pescalgarve, Flavobacteriales, Cytophagales, and Pseudomonadales share the dominance at all diel phases. The mean relative abundance of each order appears to be relatively stable across all diel phases in both environments, with the exception of the order Bacillales. This order of bacteria is found in low levels at dawn, noon, and dusk, but they have a peak at midnight. Midnight is the time point of nocturnal respiration. This group is possibly recruited for their function in this metabolic process.

### Figure 5.2 Heatmap of relative abundance patterns

This heatmap displays the relative abundance patterns of the top 30 bacterial genera associated with the *Ulva* epibiome across four diel phases (Dawn, Noon, Dusk, and Midnight) and both sites. The abundances are standardized across rows using the Z-score. A dark red box signifies strong relative enrichment abundance of the genus (Z ≥ +2) , white is the mean baseline abundance (Z ≈ 0), and dark blue is a strong relative depletion (Z ≤ -2). The genera are grouped by hierarchical clustering based on similar spatial and temporal abundance profiles over a 24-hour cycle.

```{r 19_ulva_heatmap}

# Filter Ulva samples 
ulva_clean2 <- lumilettuce                                                      |>
  filter(
    superkingdom            == "Bacteria",
    sample_type             == "Ulva",
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    !is.na(genus),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    count > 0
  )                                                                             |>
  # Sum duplicate entries per genus within each sample
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, genus)                             |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Identify the top 30 most abundant genera on Ulva
top_genera <- ulva_clean2                                                       |>
  group_by(genus)                                                               |>
  summarise(total_count = sum(count), .groups = "drop")                         |>
  slice_max(order_by = total_count, n = 30)                                     |>
  pull(genus)

# Calculate the mean relative abundance (%) per site and diel phase
ulva_rel <- ulva_clean2                                                         |>
  filter(genus %in% top_genera)                                                 |>
  group_by(sample_id)                                                           |>
  mutate(rel_abund = (count / sum(count)) * 100)                                |>
  ungroup()

# Average across biological replicates for each condition
heat_df <- ulva_rel                                                             |>
  group_by(genus, site_name, diel_phase)                                        |>
  summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_abund, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")         |>
  complete(genus, site_name, diel_phase, fill = list(mean_rel = 0))

# Construct matrix & calculate row-wise Z-scores
heat_wide <- heat_df                                                            |>
  mutate(
    col_id = paste(site_name, diel_phase, sep = "__")
  )                                                                             |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols     = genus,
    names_from  = col_id,
    values_from = mean_rel
  )                                                                             |>
  column_to_rownames("genus")                                                   |>
  as.matrix()

# Reorder columns chronologically per site
ordered_cols <- c(
  paste("Pescalgarve", c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight"), sep = "__"),
  paste("Ria de Alvor", c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight"), sep = "__")
)
heat_wide <- heat_wide[, ordered_cols]

z_matrix <- t(scale(t(heat_wide)))

z_matrix[is.nan(z_matrix)] <- 0


col_meta <- tibble(col_id = colnames(z_matrix)) |>
  separate(col_id, into = c("Site", "Diel_Phase"), sep = "__")

# Define categorical palette
site_colors <- c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6")
diel_colors <- c(
  "Midnight"                = "#2C3E50", # Dark navy
  "Dawn"                    = "#E67E22", # Orange sunrise
  "Noon"                    = "#F1C40F", # Bright yellow
  "Dusk"                    = "#9B59B6"  # Purple dusk
)

top_anno <- HeatmapAnnotation(
  `Site Name`               = col_meta$Site,
  `Diel Phase`              = factor(col_meta$Diel_Phase),
  col = list(
    `Site Name`             = site_colors,
    `Diel Phase`            = diel_colors
  ),
  annotation_name_side      = "left",
  annotation_legend_param   = list(
    `Site Name`             = list(title = "Site Name", title_gp = gpar(fontface = "bold")),
    `Diel Phase`            = list(title = "Diel Phase", title_gp = gpar(fontface = "bold"))
  )
)

# Diverging color gradient for Z-scores (Blue -> White -> Red)
col_fun <- colorRamp2(c(-2, 0, 2), c("#2166AC", "#F7F7F7", "#B2182B"))

# Plot the heatmap
ht <- Heatmap(
  z_matrix,
  name                      = "Row Z-score",
  col                       = col_fun,
  top_annotation            = top_anno,
  column_split              = col_meta$Site, 
  cluster_columns           = FALSE,         # Keep chronological 24-hour cycle intact
  cluster_rows              = TRUE,          
  clustering_distance_rows  = "euclidean",
  clustering_method_rows    = "complete",
  show_column_names         = TRUE,
  column_labels             = col_meta$Diel_Phase,
  column_names_rot          = 45,
  column_names_gp           = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold"),
  row_names_gp              = gpar(fontsize = 9, fontitalic = TRUE),
  rect_gp                   = gpar(col = "white", lwd = 0.5), 
  heatmap_legend_param      = list(
    title_gp                = gpar(fontface = "bold"),
    legend_height           = unit(4, "cm")
  )
)


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
png("../output/figures/ulva_heatmap.png", width = 9.5, height = 11, units = "in", res = 300)
draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "right", annotation_legend_side = "right")
dev.off()

draw(ht)

```

The enriched genera in Pescalgarve are in the lower half of the heatmap, whereas they are in the upper half of the heatmap for Ria de Alvor.

*Bacillus* shows high relative enrichment at midnight in both sites, and drops sharply during daytime. There is a dawn bloom at Ria de Alvor at dawn composed of : *Pseudoalteromonas*, *Vibrio*, and *Alteromonas*. The genera *Glaciecola*, *Marinagarivoran*s, and *Acinetobacter* spike at noon in Ria de Alvor, whereas they decrease at that same timepoint in Pescalgarve. At dusk, *Rhodobacteraceae* surges at Pescalgarve along with *Hyphomonadaceae_uncultured* and *Escherichia-Shigell*a at Ria de Alvor.

### Table 5.1 PERMANOVA community table

This PERMANOVA uses the 'adonis2' function from the 'vegan' package to evaluate whether whole bacterial community composition changes across sampling site and diel phases. This is a two-way model which can look at the two factors, site name and diel phase, and their interaction.

To avoid false positives caused by unequal dispersion, the assumption of homogeniety of multivariate dispersion must be met. The p-value must be greater than 0.05.

If the interaction term is non-significant, the interaction term will be dropped and an additive model will be run to obtain the exact values for the main effects, as is best practice in statistical analysis.

```{r 20_permanova_community}

# Extract matching metadata
metadata_ulva <- ulva_clean2                                                    |>
  distinct(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase)                                    |>
  mutate(
    diel_phase           = factor(diel_phase),
    site_name            = factor(site_name, levels = c("Pescalgarve", "Ria de Alvor"))
  )                                                                             |>
  arrange(sample_id)

# Pivot into a numeric community matrix 
comm_matrix_ulva <- ulva_clean2                                                 |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus)                                                    |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")                 |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols              = sample_id,
    names_from           = genus,
    values_from          = count,
    values_fill          = 0
  )                                                                             |>
  arrange(sample_id)                                                            |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")                                               |>
  as.matrix()

# Verify alignment
stopifnot(identical(rownames(comm_matrix_ulva), metadata_ulva$sample_id))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Compute dissimilarity matrices
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A. Bray-Curtis (abundance-weighted)
dist_bc <- vegdist(comm_matrix_ulva, method = "bray")

# B. Jaccard (incidence / presence-absence)
dist_jacc <- vegdist(comm_matrix_ulva, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two-way factorial PERMANOVA (adonis2)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: BRAY-CURTIS ===================\n")
permanova_bc <- adonis2(
  dist_bc ~ site_name * diel_phase,
  data                   = metadata_ulva,
  permutations           = 999,
  by                     = "margin"
)
print(permanova_bc)

cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: JACCARD ===================\n")
permanova_jacc <- adonis2(
  dist_jacc ~ site_name * diel_phase,
  data                   = metadata_ulva,
  permutations           = 999,
  by                     = "margin"
)
print(permanova_jacc)

# Multivariate dispersion (betadisper)
disp_site <- betadisper(dist_bc, metadata_ulva$site_name)
cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Site Name ---\n")
print(anova(disp_site))

disp_diel <- betadisper(dist_bc, metadata_ulva$diel_phase)
cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Diel Phase ---\n")
print(anova(disp_diel))

# Additive model to test main effects of site and diel phase
fit_bc <- adonis2(dist_bc ~ site_name + diel_phase, data = metadata_ulva, permutations = 999, by = "margin")
fit_jacc <- adonis2(dist_jacc ~ site_name + diel_phase, data = metadata_ulva, permutations = 999, by = "margin")

# Create table 
tidy_adonis <- function(mod, metric_name) {
  as_tibble(mod, rownames = "Factor")                                           |>
    mutate(
      Metric = metric_name,
      Factor = dplyr::recode(Factor,
        "site_name"      = "Site Name",
        "diel_phase"     = "Diel Phase",
        "Residual"       = "Residuals",
        "Total"          = "Total"
      )
    )                                                                           |>
    dplyr::rename(
      Df                 = Df,
      SumOfSqs           = SumOfSqs,
      R2                 = R2,
      F_stat             = F,
      p_val              = `Pr(>F)`
    )                                                                           |>
    relocate(Metric, Factor)
}

# Combine both metrics
permanova_table_df <- bind_rows(
  tidy_adonis(fit_bc, "Bray-Curtis"),
  tidy_adonis(fit_jacc, "Jaccard")
)

# Format with `gt`
permanova_gt <- permanova_table_df                                              |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Metric")                                                  |>
  cols_label(
    Factor               = md("**Source of Variation**"),
    Df                   = md("**Df**"),
    SumOfSqs             = md("**Sum of Squares**"),
    R2                   = md("**R²**"),
    F_stat               = md("**Pseudo-F**"),
    p_val                = md("**p-value**")
  )                                                                             |>
  fmt_number(columns = SumOfSqs, decimals = 3)                                  |>
  fmt_number(columns = R2, decimals = 3)                                        |>
  fmt_number(columns = F_stat, decimals = 2)                                    |>
  fmt_number(columns = p_val, decimals = 3)                                     |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")                                               |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.names = "Arial",
    table.font.size = px(13),
    heading.align = "left",
    row_group.font.weight = "bold"
  )
# print(permanova_gt)

# gtsave(permanova_gt, "../output/tables/permanova_community.png")
```

There is no interaction between site name and diel phase according to both distance metrics (Bray-Curtis: F3,64 = 0.68, R2 = 0.026, p-value = 0.916; Jaccard: F3,64 = 0.87, R2 = 0.035, p-value = 0.753). This suggests that the diel changes of the microbiome do not significantly diverge between sites. In other words, The diurnal temporal patterns are not significantly different in the aquaculture facility compared to the natural coastal lagoon.

For the homogeneity of multivariate dispersion, the assumption is met for both variables (site name and diel phase) which confirms that the PERMANOVA tests are robust and unbiased.

The additive model reveals sampling site to be a significant driver of the *Ulva* microbiome. Indeed, the epibiome differs both in abundance-weighted composition (Bray-Curtis) and membership/turnover (Jaccard). The effect size is larger in Bray-Curtis than in Jaccard (R2: 11.62% \> 8.13%), indicating that site differentiation is primarily driven by shifts in the relative abundances of shared core bacterial genera as well as some taxon replacement. As for diel phase, the model shows whole-community diel stability. Over a 24-hour cycle, the baseline composition remains resilient and stable (p-values \> 0.5).

### 4. Differential abundance analysis

The differential abundance analysis will reveal which bacterial genera are significantly enriched during the daytime light peak (Noon) versus the nocturnal phase (Midnight). The method used is the ANCOM-BC2 because it is the gold standard for compositional sequencing count data and adjusts for sampling depth while accounting for covariates (site name). Basically, this method accounts for sampling fraction differences, handles zero inflation, and includes site name as a covariate.

```{r 21_differential_abundance}

diel_clean <- lumilettuce                                                      |>
  filter(
    superkingdom            == "Bacteria",
    sample_type             == "Ulva",
    diel_phase %in% c("Midnight", "Noon"),
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(genus),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    count > 0
  )                                                                             |>
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, genus)                             |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Build numeric count matrix 
count_mat <- diel_clean                                                         |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols                 = genus,
    names_from              = sample_id,
    values_from             = count,
    values_fill             = 0
  )                                                                             |>
  column_to_rownames("genus")                                                   |>
  as.matrix()

# Build metadata aligned with columns of count_mat
sample_meta <- diel_clean                                                       |>
  distinct(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase)                                    |>
  mutate(
    diel_phase              = factor(diel_phase, levels = c("Midnight", "Noon")),
    site_name               = factor(site_name, levels = c("Pescalgarve", "Ria de Alvor"))
  )                                                                             |>
  arrange(match(sample_id, colnames(count_mat)))                                |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# Verify sample matching
stopifnot(identical(colnames(count_mat), rownames(sample_meta)))

# Construct TreeSummarizedExperiment
tse <- TreeSummarizedExperiment(
  assays                    = list(counts = count_mat),
  colData                   = DataFrame(sample_meta)
)

# Run ANCOM-BC2 
ancom_res <- ancombc2(
  data                      = tse,
  assay_name                = "counts",
  tax_level                 = NULL,
  fix_formula               = "site_name + diel_phase",
  p_adj_method              = "BH",
  prv_cut                   = 0.10, # Filter taxa absent in > 90% of samples
  group                     = "diel_phase",
  struc_zero                = TRUE,
  neg_lb                    = TRUE
)

# Extract Differentially Abundant Taxa
res_df <- ancom_res$res                                                         |>
  select(
    taxon,
    lfc_Noon                = lfc_diel_phaseNoon,
    se_Noon                 = se_diel_phaseNoon,
    W_Noon                  = W_diel_phaseNoon,
    p_Noon                  = p_diel_phaseNoon,
    q_Noon                  = q_diel_phaseNoon,
    diff_Noon               = diff_diel_phaseNoon
  )                                                                             |>
  arrange(q_Noon)

# Filter statistically significant taxa 
sig_genera <- res_df                                                            |>
  filter(diff_Noon == TRUE, q_Noon < 0.05)                                      |>
  mutate(
    Enrichment = if_else(lfc_Noon > 0, "Noon (Light Peak)", "Midnight (Dark)")
  )                                                                             |>
  arrange(desc(lfc_Noon))

print(head(sig_genera, 15))
```

The table returns 0 rows because no bacterial genus reached the strict false discovery rate cutoff (q_Noon \< 0.05) after Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) multiple testing correction across all tested genera. This aligns with the findings of the PERMANOVA, supporting the fact that the whole community does not experience a massive turnover across diel phases.

We can restrict testing to taxa present in at least 30% of samples to drastically reduce the correction burden. Filtering out the rare or sporadic taxa will reduce the statistical noise and is standard practice in microbiome bioinformatics. In this model, midnight is the baseline diel phase such that the Log2 fold change of Noon is relative to midnight.

A positive LFC = enrichment at noon,

A negative LFC = enrichment at midnight

```{r 22_prevalent_taxa}

# Identify the prevalent taxa which is present in >= 30% of samples
prevalent_taxa <- diel_clean                                                    |>
  group_by(genus)                                                               |>
  summarise(prevalence = n_distinct(sample_id) / 36)                            |>
  filter(prevalence >= 0.30)                                                    |>
  pull(genus)

# Run ANCOM-BC2 on this set
tse_core <- tse[rownames(tse) %in% prevalent_taxa, ]

ancom_core <- ancombc2(
  data                  = tse_core,
  assay_name            = "counts",
  tax_level             = NULL,
  fix_formula           = "site_name + diel_phase",
  p_adj_method          = "BH",
  group                 = "diel_phase",
  struc_zero            = TRUE,
  neg_lb                = TRUE
)

# Extract the results
res_core <- ancom_core$res                                                      |>
  select(
    taxon,
    lfc_Noon            = lfc_diel_phaseNoon,
    se_Noon             = se_diel_phaseNoon,
    W_Noon              = W_diel_phaseNoon,
    p_Noon              = p_diel_phaseNoon,
    q_Noon              = q_diel_phaseNoon,
    diff_Noon           = diff_diel_phaseNoon
  )                                                                             |>
  arrange(p_Noon)

# Prepare top 20 candidate taxa for table
table_ancom_data <- res_core                                                    |>
  slice_head(n = 20)                                                            |>
  mutate(
    # Format numeric values
    lfc_Noon            = sprintf("%.2f", lfc_Noon),
    se_Noon             = sprintf("%.2f", se_Noon),
    W_Noon              = sprintf("%.2f", W_Noon),
    # Format p and q values
    p_Noon              = if_else(p_Noon < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_Noon)),
    q_Noon              = if_else(q_Noon < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", q_Noon)),
    # Recode significance logical flag
    diff_Noon           = if_else(diff_Noon == TRUE, "Yes", "No")
  )

ancom_table <- table_ancom_data |>
  select(taxon, lfc_Noon, se_Noon, W_Noon, p_Noon, q_Noon) |>
  flextable() |>
  set_header_labels(
    taxon    = "Taxon (Genus)",
    lfc_Noon = "Log2 Fold Change",
    se_Noon  = "SE",
    W_Noon   = "W",
    p_Noon   = "p-value",
    q_Noon   = "q-value (FDR)"
  ) |>
  bold(part = "header") |>
  autofit()

# ancom_table

# dir.create("../output/tables", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
# 
# flextable::save_as_image(
#   x    = ancom_table,
#   path = "../output/tables/ancom_core_noon_summary.png",
#   zoom = 3
# )
```

Several taxa show marked shifts in effect size and unadjusted significance (p \< 0.01). Nocturnal enrichment (negative log-fold change (lfc)) was most pronounced in *Methylotenera* (LFC = -1.122, unadjusted p = 0.0004, q = 0.094) and *Bacillus* (LFC = -1.312, unadjusted p = 0.0019, q = 0.238). The peak midday irradiance favored *Sphingobacterium* (LFC = 0.767, unadjusted p = 0.0090, q = 0.251), *Algitalea* (LFC = 0.704, unadjusted p = 0.0129, q = 0.303), *Planktomarina* (LFC = 0.647, unadjusted p = 0.0079, q = 0.251), and *uncultured Marinifilaceae* (LFC = 0.637, unadjusted p = 0.0057, q = 0.251).

## VI. Indicator taxa across niches and diel phases

### Test 6.1 Indicator taxa analysis

The function used calculates the Dufrêne-Legendre Indicator Value (IndVal), which is the square root of the product of component A and component B. In this case, component A is specificity/relative abundance, the probability that a sample belongs to the target group given that the bacterial genus has been detected. If the value is equal to 1.0, this means that the genus has only been found in that specific group and in no other group. Component B is fidelity/relative frequency, the probability of finding the genus in samples belonging to the target group. A value equal to 1.0 suggests that the genus is present in 100% of samples of that group. If :

IndVal ≥ 0.7 : strong, highly diagnostic indicator

0.5 ≤ IndVal \< 0.7 : moderate indicator taxon

IndVal \< 0.5 : weak indicator taxon

```{r 23_indicator_df}

# A. Sample Type: Ulva vs. Water Filter 
ind_type <- multipatt(
  comm_all,
  meta_all$sample_type,
  control               = how(nperm = 999),
  func                  = "IndVal.g",
  duleg                 = TRUE # force test to evaluate groups separately
)

# B. Site Name: Pescalgarve vs. Ria de Alvor 
ind_site <- multipatt(
  comm_ulva,
  meta_ulva$site_name,
  control               = how(nperm = 999),
  func                  = "IndVal.g",
  duleg                 = TRUE
)

# C. Diel Phase: Dawn vs. Noon vs. Dusk vs. Midnight 
ind_diel <- multipatt(
  comm_ulva,
  meta_ulva$diel_phase,
  control               = how(nperm = 999),
  func                  = "IndVal.g",
  duleg                 = TRUE
)

# Helper function to extract indicators
extract_indicators <- function(ind_obj, factor_name) {
  sign_df <- as.data.frame(ind_obj$sign)                                       |>
    rownames_to_column("genus")                                                |>
    filter(!is.na(p.value), p.value < 0.05)

  if (nrow(sign_df) == 0) {
    return(tibble(
      Factor            = character(),
      Associated_Group  = character(),
      genus             = character(),
      IndVal            = numeric(),
      p.value           = numeric()
    ))
  }

  # Identify the indicator columns (excluding 'index', 'stat', and 'p.value')
  group_cols <- setdiff(colnames(ind_obj$sign), c("index", "stat", "p.value"))

  # Vectorized identification of which group each genus belongs to
  group_labels <- apply(sign_df[, group_cols, drop = FALSE], 1, function(vals) {
    matched <- group_cols[which(vals == 1)]
    clean_matched <- sub("^s\\.", "", matched)
    if (length(clean_matched) == 1) {
      return(clean_matched)
    } else if (length(clean_matched) > 1) {
      return(paste(clean_matched, collapse = " + "))
    } else {
      return("None")
    }
  })

  tibble(
    Factor              = factor_name,
    Associated_Group    = group_labels,
    genus               = sign_df$genus,
    IndVal              = sign_df$stat,
    p.value             = sign_df$p.value
  )                                                                            |>
    arrange(desc(IndVal))
}

# Run extraction
df_type_ind <- extract_indicators(ind_type, "Sample Type")
df_site_ind <- extract_indicators(ind_site, "Site Name")
df_diel_ind <- extract_indicators(ind_diel, "Diel Phase")

# Combine into master table
all_indicators_df <- bind_rows(df_type_ind, df_site_ind, df_diel_ind)

head(all_indicators_df, 15)
```

Question 1: Which bacteria are true epiphyes/endophytes vs. free-living pelagic bacterioplankton?

This can be answered looking at sample type.

Question 2: How does the environment shape the host-associated microbiome?

This can be answered looking at site name variable.

Question 3: Are there specific taxa that respond to daily day/night metabolic cycles despite the overall community stability?

This can be answered looking at the diel phase variable.

### Table 6.1 Indicator table

The table below will be included in the thesis manuscript to present the answer to the above questions. It will only present the top 5 bacterial genera for each target group.

```{r 24_indicator_table}
# Filter top indicators per group for presentation
table_indicators <- all_indicators_df                                           |>
  group_by(Factor, Associated_Group)                                            |>
  slice_max(order_by = IndVal, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE)                        |>
  ungroup()                                                                     |>
  arrange(Factor, Associated_Group, desc(IndVal))

# Calculate row grouping counts for Factor
factor_counts <- table(forcats::fct_inorder(table_indicators$Factor))

indicator_table <- table_indicators                                             |>
  select(Associated_Group, genus, IndVal, p.value)                              |>
  kbl(
    col.names         = c("Target Group", "Bacterial Genus", "IndVal Statistic", "p-value"),
    digits            = 3,
    align             = c("l", "l", "c", "c"),
  )                                                                             |>
  kable_classic(
    full_width        = FALSE,
    html_font         = "Arial",
    font_size         = 13
  )                                                                             |>
  column_spec(2, italic = TRUE)                                                 |>
  pack_rows(index = factor_counts)
```
